claims.text: Veeam Kasten 9.0.2              day-two operations
Explain how Kubernetes and distribution version support sets the pace of your upgrade calendar
Collect the right diagnostics before you open a support case

Two differences change the calendar more than anything else in this module. First, cadence: Veeam Kasten ships far more frequently than a Veeam Data Platform release cycle — the product documentation's own maintenance guidance is to always upgrade and not stay on an outdated version for comfort, noting releases every two weeks [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1093]. Second, the floor moves: Veeam Kasten supports a defined list of Kubernetes and OpenShift versions and does not support distribution versions that are no longer actively supported by their vendor or community [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.861

The catalog is the product.                    Restore points are only useful while something knows they exist. Veeam Kasten Disaster Recovery exists to protect that catalog, and catalog storage space is also what gates your upgrades [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1093].
Upgrade the Helm release in the Veeam Kasten namespace, reusing your current values [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.199]
Two constraints have no console equivalent: upgrades are supported across a maximum of four versions, and at least 50% free space is required in catalog storage [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.198]
Read the dashboard's compliance states, then the action metrics behind them [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.301, p.748]
Alerting is something you wire up: Veeam Kasten exposes a Prometheus endpoint for a central system to extract data from [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.746]
Enable the Veeam Kasten Disaster Recovery (KDR) policy, which backs up Veeam Kasten's own resources and catalog to a location profile [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.565, p.571]
Recovery depends on a passphrase you stored and a location profile configured on the target cluster [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.571, p.572]
Let the garbage collector clean up resources that are orphaned or past their expiration period [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.839]
Retiring a restore point does not always free space right away, and deduplication can make the reclamation minimal [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.365]

Three of the four day-two duties in that table — upgrades, dashboard health, and catalog protection — all touch catalog storage. If you take one number away from this module, take 50%: the free space Veeam Kasten needs in catalog storage for upgrades [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1093].

This section gives you the upgrade rules, the command that performs the upgrade, and a planner you can use to decide whether your instance is one hop or several hops from current. It also covers the version support you do not control: the Kubernetes and OpenShift releases underneath you.

Veeam Kasten upgrades are supported across a maximum of four versions (for example, 2.0.10 to 2.0.14). If your instance is further behind, a step upgrade process is recommended, using the       --version        flag with       helm upgrade        to control the version jumps — and at least 50% free space is required in catalog storage [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.198].

You do not have to work the arithmetic out by hand. You can verify available catalog free space and see your recommended upgrade path from the System Information page under the Settings menu in the navigation sidebar [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.198]. From a terminal you can ask the same question with       k10tools        — get the binary before you need it, since it is a separate download rather than something the Helm chart installs for you: Veeam Kasten publishes       k10tools        for Linux, macOS, and Windows, and the current release is linked from the Veeam Kasten Tools page in the prod

A release may perform a catalog schema upgrade, and the schema upgrade requires at least 50% of free space in the       catalog-pv-claim        persistent volume — the claim's size may need to be increased first. Available catalog storage space is visible in the dashboard under Settings > System Information > Upgrade Status [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1097].

An upgrade is a Helm upgrade of the release you installed, run against the namespace you installed into — the documented example assumes the       kasten-io        namespace and the release name       k10        [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.199]. The documented sequence refreshes the chart repository, captures your current values, and upgrades using them, so your configuration survives the upgrade [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.200].

For a step upgrade, the same sequence carries a pinned version — this is the form the upgrade primer prints as its recommended upgrade path, with the target release on the end [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.872].

Read the Upgrade Notes for every release you pass through, not only the one you land on — that is where the breaking details live. Recent examples: an       app_namespace        label was added to per-application metrics, so Prometheus queries that pin the exact label set may need updating [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1097]; metrics sourced through Red Hat ACM Observability moved from       cluster_id        to       cluster_uid       , so dashboards and alert rules filtering on the old label need changing [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1099]; and policy, profile, and action names became limited to 63

Answer both questions the way your cluster looks today, then plan the upgrade. The planner applies only the two documented rules: the four-version support window and the catalog free-space requirement [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.198].

The other half of staying current is the platform underneath. Veeam Kasten publishes the certified Kubernetes distributions and respective OpenShift versions it supports, and does not support distribution versions that are no longer actively supported by their vendor or community [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.861]. A single Veeam Kasten release can move both ends of that list: release 8.5.9 added support for Kubernetes 1.34 [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1098] and, in the same release, removed support for Kubernetes 1.30 while OpenShift 4.17 clusters continued to be supported [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.
1.34                                        4.21                            Supported [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.862]
1.33                                        4.20                            Supported [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.862]
1.32                                        4.19                            Supported [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.862]
1.31                                        4.18                            Supported [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.862]
1.30                                        4.17                            Kubernetes version     only      supported when deployed as an OpenShift cluster [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.862]
1.29                                        4.16                            Kubernetes version     only      supported when deployed as an OpenShift cluster [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.862]

Put the cluster's Kubernetes upgrade on the same calendar as the Veeam Kasten upgrade, and sequence them deliberately. Veeam Kasten supports a published list of Kubernetes and OpenShift versions and does not support distribution versions that are no longer actively supported by their vendor or community [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.861, p.862], and a single release can add one version and remove another [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1098, p.1099] — so if the platform team moves the cluster first, your options narrow to whichever Veeam Kasten release supports the new version, while upgrading Veeam Kas

This section takes you from the morning glance to the support case: the three layers of monitoring available to you, the alerts worth creating first, and the order to gather diagnostics in when something looks wrong.

The top of the Veeam Kasten dashboard shows the applications on the cluster, the policies that exist, and a summary of the cluster's backup data footprint [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.301]. Filtered to applications with stateful services, each is placed in one of four states — the closest thing here to your morning read of job sessions [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.301].
Unmanaged        No protection policy covers this object [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.301].
Non-compliant        A policy applies, but its actions are failing or have not been invoked yet — for example, right after policy creation [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.301].
Compliant        A policy applies and its service-level agreements (SLAs) are being respected [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.301].
Removed        Objects that no longer exist on the cluster; filter to this state to find a removed application and restore it [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.301, p.397].

Veeam Kasten enables centralized monitoring of its activity by integrating with Prometheus, exposing a Prometheus endpoint that a central system can extract data from [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.746]. The built-in instance is configured by default with persistent storage of 8Gi and a retention period of 30d, changeable through the       prometheus.server.persistentVolume.size        and       prometheus.server.retention        Helm values [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.746].

Leave that server enabled. Disabling it reduces functionality in various parts of the system, including usage data, reporting, and the multi-cluster dashboard; if it has been disabled, it can be re-enabled during a Helm upgrade with       --set prometheus.server.enabled=true        [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.763].

Action metrics are the ones you will query first. Veeam Kasten records counts for cluster and application-specific actions, labels them with the action's context, and includes the final status as       state        for ended actions — with an action's state reported as values including       pending       ,       running       ,       attempt_failed       ,       failed       ,       succeeded       ,       cancelled       ,       skipped       , and       deleting        [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.748].
PromQL · successful backups in the past 24 hours

Read it as: how many backup actions finished successfully in the last 24 hours.       action_ended_total        is the metric name; the curly braces filter to backup actions that succeeded;       [24h]        is the lookback window;       increase        counts how many happened inside it;       sum        and       round        collapse that down to one tidy number.

Swap the labels and you have the query that matters more:       sum(round(increase(action_ended_total{action="restore",state="failed"}[1h])))        returns failed restores in the past hour [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.748].

Metrics can leave the cluster two ways: Prometheus remote write pushes them to remote Prometheus-compatible endpoints such as Grafana, Datadog, or Thanos, and external Prometheus integration has an outside Prometheus instance scrape the built-in server — remote write is documented as the recommended route for most use cases [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.754]. Grafana then visualizes what Prometheus collected, and alerts fire when metrics cross the levels you care about [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1093]. In most organizations that central Prometheus/Grafana stack belongs to a platform or observabilit

The product's own guidance is to create alerts for any actions where       state=failed       , and for Catalog Volume Used Space > 50%, because that condition could impact Veeam Kasten upgrades [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1093]. The second one is the link back to Section 02: the alert that protects your upgrade window. For version tracking from an external monitor, the       k10_build_info        Prometheus gauge metric exposes the running Veeam Kasten version as a label [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1099].
From "that looks wrong" to a support case

Confirm which actions are failing and on which applications, using the compliance states and the action list. A non-compliant application tells you a policy's actions are failing or have not run yet [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.301].
Download the support logs from the dashboard
Admin users running 4.5.7 or later can get support logs from the System Information page under the Settings menu in the navigation sidebar — no terminal required [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.862].

The debug script generates a compressed archive,       k10_debug_logs.tar.gz       , containing separate log files for the Veeam Kasten services; it assumes your default context points at the cluster and that Veeam Kasten is installed in the       kasten-io        namespace, and option flags exist for a different namespace or output file [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.862]. It can also gather metrics from the Prometheus server installed by Veeam Kasten when you pass       --prom-duration       ; the duration drives the size of the captured data, and       --prom-metrics-only        separates metric

The       k10tools        binary has commands that help validate whether a cluster is set up correctly before installing Veeam Kasten and debug the Veeam Kasten micro services [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.864]. Storage class validation is available the same way, and admin users can validate storage classes from the System Information page of the Settings menu — the state "Unknown" is shown until validation is run [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.864].

Support runs through Veeam Kasten Community Support or a case opened at the Veeam customer portal [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.861]. Collecting the bundle first is what turns a case into a diagnosis instead of a request for logs.

Source: Veeam Kasten 9.0.2 user guide, p.862. The collected logs also contain a Prometheus health-check section with a curated set of metrics for evaluating the storage and retention health of the Prometheus instance [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.863].

Veeam Kasten is a stateful application running on the cluster, so it must be responsible for backing up its own data to enable recovery in the event of disaster — the backup enabled by the Veeam Kasten Disaster Recovery (KDR) policy [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.565]. KDR provides the ability to recover the Veeam Kasten platform from a variety of disasters: unintended deletion of Veeam Kasten or its restore points, failure of the underlying storage used by Veeam Kasten, or accidental destruction of the Kubernetes cluster Veeam Kasten is deployed on [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.565]. The API exposes t

The Veeam Data Platform parallel is configuration backup, and it holds up well: both protect the metadata that makes restore points findable, both are scheduled, and both are worthless if you cannot decrypt them. Where it breaks is the dependency list. The guide is blunt about what to retain after enabling KDR, without which restore point catalog recovery will not be possible: the source Cluster ID, the KDR passphrase or the external secret manager details, and the KDR location profile details and credential [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.585].

Where you turn it on.          The Veeam Kasten Disaster Recovery settings are on the Setup Kasten DR page under the Settings menu in the navigation sidebar; you specify a location profile for the exported KDR backups and choose the passphrase method used to encrypt them [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.571, p.572]. Note the sidebar: Restore Kasten sits directly below it, which is the page you will use on the far side of a disaster.

Choose a location profile that supports immutable backups — the guide states this strongly, so that restore point catalog data can be recovered in the event of incidents including ransomware and accidental deletion [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.571]. And check your intended target: Veeam Repository location profiles cannot be used as a destination for KDR backups [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.572]. Passphrase options include a passphrase you supply, HashiCorp Vault, and AWS Secrets Manager [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.572]; Azure Key Vault Secrets was added as a passphrase provider for Disaster Recovery,

The KDR mode specifies how internal Veeam Kasten resources are protected. It must be set before enabling the KDR policy, and changes to the mode only apply to future KDR policy runs [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.565]. Starting in Veeam Kasten v8.0.0, all installations default to Quick DR (Local Catalog Snapshot) mode — a mode that should only be enabled if the storage provisioner used for Veeam Kasten persistent volume claims supports both creating storage snapshots and restoring the existing volume from one [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.565].
Storage used for Veeam Kasten persistent volume claims supports both creating storage snapshots and provisioning a volume from a snapshot [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.568]
Creates a local snapshot of the catalog persistent volume claim and incrementally exports only the minimally required catalog data [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.568]

Storage can create snapshots but cannot provision a volume from one; or you want to reduce local snapshot retention without affecting exported backups. May be selected on any snapshot-capable storage for the highest level of resilience [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.568]
Everything the local-snapshot mode does, plus an incremental export of the catalog snapshot data [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.568]
No available cluster storage supports snapshot creation, or there is no requirement to recover local restore points or action history [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.569, p.570]
Incrementally exports only the minimally required catalog data; does not support recovery of local restore points and action history [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.570]

Supported for backwards-compatibility only — the mode is deprecated and will be removed in a future release, and all clusters should be migrated to a supported Quick DR configuration [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.566, p.567]
Exports a full copy of the catalog database [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.567]

Quick DR modes protect additional Veeam Kasten resource types compared with Legacy DR, including policy presets, transform sets, blueprint bindings, and basic user policies; reports, action pod specs, and audit configuration are protected by neither [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.570]. If your storage cannot take or restore local snapshots, Legacy mode is selected explicitly with the Helm value       kastenDisasterRecovery.quickMode.enabled=false        [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.566].

Enabling KDR creates a dedicated policy that backs up Veeam Kasten's resources and catalog data to an external location profile [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.571]. That policy is named       k10-disaster-recovery-policy       , is created automatically when KDR is enabled, and can be viewed through the Policies page in the navigation sidebar; Run Once starts a manual backup, and Edit changes the frequency and retention [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.587]. The frequency guidance is worth writing down: the KDR policy should match the frequency of the lowest recovery point objective (RPO) policy on the cl

The policy you did not create, and should still review.          Frequency and retention are editable, and the location profile shown here is an immutable one [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.571, p.587]. If you recognize this layout from your own application policies, that is the point — KDR is a policy like any other, pointed at Veeam Kasten's own namespace.

Stage 01 — export off-site.          The documented rebuild strategy starts by configuring policies to export backups to an off-site location [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1093]. Without this, KDR recovers a catalog that points at data the surviving site cannot read.

Stage 02 — protect the catalog.          Enable Disaster Recovery for Veeam Kasten to export the Veeam Kasten catalog to external storage, using a user-provided passphrase key or third-party management of the secret that encrypts the catalog data [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1093].

Stage 03 — new cluster.          In the event of a complete cluster or site loss, a new cluster can be deployed in a secondary site or the public cloud [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1093]. This is the stage where the rebuild strategy pays its cost in time — the tradeoff documented against the replicate strategy, which pre-seeds a secondary site instead [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1093].

Stage 04 — redeploy.          Veeam Kasten can be redeployed via Helm, and a location profile created to point to the off-site data repository [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1093]. This is Module 03's install, run against an empty cluster — which is the argument for having practiced it.

Stage 05 — import the catalog.          The Veeam Kasten catalog can be imported, via the previously set passphrase, to the new instance of Veeam Kasten [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1093]. In the dashboard this is the Restore Kasten page, which asks for the location profile holding the exported KDR backups, the cluster identifier of the source instance, and the passphrase method used at setup [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.571, p.572].

Stage 05 in the dashboard.          Recovering an instance asks for the location profile, the cluster identifier of the source instance, and the passphrase used when the KDR policy was configured — then a restore point and a summary [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.571, p.572]. Every field on this screen is something you decided months earlier, which is why the passphrase belongs in your secrets store and your runbook, not in someone's memory.

Veeam Kasten catalog backup and restore are handled through this dedicated disaster recovery process, and the guide's recommendation is to enable Veeam Kasten DR and regularly test the process [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1093]. Treat the KDR test like the restore tests you already run: on a schedule, with the passphrase retrieved from where it is meant to live rather than from your own notes.

"Who backs up the backup system?" is the question that ends a lot of Kubernetes protection projects late. The answer here is concrete and demonstrable: the platform runs a dedicated policy over its own namespace, exports the catalog to an external location profile you choose — one that supports immutable backups, so the catalog survives ransomware and accidental deletion — and encrypts it with a passphrase held in a passphrase provider, then recovers onto a new cluster from that export [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.565, p.571, p.1093].

Veeam Kasten provides a way to collect and clean up resources that are either orphaned or whose expiration period has passed, through a garbage collector daemon [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.839]. Three Helm options tune it:       garbagecollector.daemonPeriod        sets the length of time between two consecutive garbage collection events in seconds,       garbagecollector.keepMaxActions        sets how many finished actions to keep — with no actions deleted if the value is less than or equal to zero — and       garbagecollector.actions.enabled        enables the action collectors [Src: Kasten Do

What the daemon cleans is a specific list: actions above the retained maximum, oldest first and handled independently per action type;       RestorePointContents        for expired manual backups, as determined by their       expiresAt        value; and the temporary objects left behind by restore operations —       CSISnapshot        objects, persistent volumes, profiles, services, network policies, secrets, and config maps [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.839]. Export pods are cleaned up by the garbage collection daemon after the configured grace period [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1097].

When restore points are retired — manually or through a policy retention schedule — Veeam Kasten cleans up the associated resources, but the cleanup is not immediate for all of them; backup data in an object store may take a significant amount of time to be removed [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.365]. Data references shared between restore points, aggregated data awaiting garbage collection, version retention for immutable backups, and safety windows for re-referencing data are among the reasons a retirement might not immediately free space, and deduplication can mean minimal or no reclamation at a

Log volume is the other thing worth setting deliberately. Log retention is tuned with Helm values including a rotation count and a size threshold that triggers rotation, applied during an upgrade of the release [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.176].
1                                   Daily                                  Read the dashboard: any application that moved to non-compliant, and any failed action [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.301].

2                                   Weekly                                  Confirm the KDR policy is running to schedule [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.587], and check catalog storage space against the 50% mark [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1093].

3                                   Monthly                                  Test restores rather than waiting for a disaster — in the same namespace, a different namespace, and a different cluster [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1093] — and test the KDR process itself [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1093].

4                                   Quarterly                                  Plan the next upgrade hop, and review the supported Kubernetes and OpenShift matrix against the cluster's roadmap [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.198, p.862].
Monitoring configuration is reviewed as the deployment evolves, so you are watching the right metrics and getting alerts for new issues [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1093].
Alerts exist for failed actions and for catalog volume used space, the two conditions the guide calls out [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1093].

The KDR passphrase is retrievable by someone other than you, from a passphrase provider rather than a personal note [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.572]. Decide who that second person or team is — security, a fellow backup admin, the secrets-management team — and write it into the runbook; "someone other than you" is a decision your team has to make explicitly, not a default the product supplies.
The upgrade path is known before the upgrade window opens, from the System Information page or the upgrade primer [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.198, p.872].

01                                     Planning an upgrade inside the four-version support window, with at least 50% free catalog storage, using the System Information page or the upgrade primer to find the path
02                                     Keeping pace with the Kubernetes and OpenShift versions Veeam Kasten supports, and sequencing cluster upgrades against product upgrades
04                                     Collecting diagnostics in order: dashboard, support logs from System Information, the debug bundle, the platform checks, then the support case
